meta.blurb: Wren Ashby only wanted her aunt to stop finding her dates. So she said she was already seeing someone, and the nearest man in the café was Kit Navarro. Six weeks, one napkin of rules and one big lantern fair. What could go wrong?
meta.bible: Wren Ashby: 29, a children's book illustrator in Salt Cove, warm, funny, shy about her work, tends to say yes to everyone. Kit Navarro: 31, the mechanic who keeps the little ferry Gannet running, quiet, dry humour, hums while he works, never says what he feels; his fiancée Dana left him two years ago. Leo: Kit's nephew, 8, lives with Kit, loves dragons and bikes. Aunt Dot: Dorothy Ashby, 70s, Wren's aunt, chairs the Lantern Fair, cannot stop matchmaking, wise and sly. Dana: Kit's ex, who comes back for one weekend. Marta: Wren's best friend, runs the bookshop. Mr Pell: owns Pell's Café, loves gossip. Ms Halden: an editor at Halden and Moss in Barrowfield. Salt Cove: a small seaside town. Barrowfield: the big city, two hours away by train. Pell's Café: where it starts. Lantern Fair: the town's night in six weeks, when paper lanterns are floated on the bay. The Sleepy Lighthouse: Wren's current picture book. Gannet: the ferry. The napkin rules: no real kissing except in public when needed; no lying to Leo; no feelings; it ends the day after the Lantern Fair. Ending: Wren takes the Halden job but works from Salt Cove; Kit and Wren are truly together; the napkin is framed at Pell's Café. Voice and tone: warm, light, funny, a slow-burning pretend romance with real feeling underneath; clean, no bad language.

B1B2: Wren Ashby spent every morning at the same table in Pell's Café, drawing animals for children's books. Salt Cove was a small town by the sea, and she had never wanted to live anywhere else.
Wren's Aunt Dot came into the café waving a piece of paper. On it were the names of five nice young men, and Dot was sure that Wren would like at least one of them.
Dot said that she had already arranged a dinner for that very evening with the new vet. Wren felt her cheeks go hot, because she had not even been asked.
At that moment the café door opened, and Kit Navarro came in with oil on his hands. He was the quiet man who kept the little ferry running, and he had only come for a coffee.
Wren heard her own voice say that she was already seeing someone. Then, because Dot asked who, she pointed at the only man in the room, and it was Kit.
Kit stood very still for a long moment, and Wren was afraid he would leave. Then he walked over, put his hand on her shoulder and said hello, darling, and Dot clapped her hands with joy.
Dot was so pleased that she invited them both to Sunday lunch. She also said that the whole town would meet Kit at the Lantern Fair, which was exactly six weeks away.
Outside, Wren said she was terribly sorry, and she explained that she had panicked. Kit was annoyed, but his mouth kept turning up at the corners, because the whole thing was very funny.
Kit thought for a moment and then said that he would help her. Since his fiancée had left two years ago, the whole town looked at him with sad eyes, and a girlfriend might stop that.
They sat down and wrote the rules on a paper napkin. Rule one said that there would be no real feelings, and rule two said that they would never lie to Kit's nephew, Leo.
The other rules said that they would kiss only in public, and only when it was really needed. The last rule said that the pretending would end on the day after the Lantern Fair.
On Sunday, they sat at Dot's big table, and Dot asked them how they had first met. They looked at each other, because they had not planned a story at all.
Kit made up a story about Wren dropping her sketchbook off the jetty, and he told it so well that everyone laughed. Wren tried to help but gave different details, and Dot's eyes narrowed a little.
After lunch, Kit's eight-year-old nephew, Leo, asked Wren a question. He wanted to know if she was really his uncle's girlfriend, and she remembered rule two and did not know what to say.
That night Wren found an email from Ms Halden, an editor at a big publishing house in the city of Barrowfield. She liked Wren's drawings and wanted her to come in for a job interview.
It rained for three days, and Kit worked on the ferry in the cold. Wren brought him hot tea in a flask, and she knew that half the town was watching them from their windows.
On Saturday, they walked through the market holding hands, because people expected it. Their hands were stiff and sweaty, and they walked like two robots.
Mr Pell from the café was standing nearby, and he shouted that they were a lovely couple. Kit quickly kissed Wren on the cheek, and both of them felt strangely shaken afterward.
Wren sat on an upturned bucket in the ferry shed and watched Kit work. She noticed that he hummed quietly, and she quickly began to sketch him in her book.
Kit found the sketch and looked at it for a long time without speaking. Then he said, quietly, that nobody had ever drawn him before, and he asked if he could keep it.
At the bookshop, Wren's friend Marta stared at her and said that she was blushing. Wren said that she was only warm, but Marta had known her for twenty years and she did not believe her.
On a calm evening, Kit let Wren hold the wheel of the ferry. He stood behind her and showed her how to turn gently, and she felt very happy and very afraid.
They sat on the harbour wall and talked about everything under the stars. It was almost midnight before they noticed, and they were both surprised that they had not run out of things to say.
One Friday, Dana, the woman who had once been engaged to Kit, came back to Salt Cove for a weekend. Everyone in the café stopped talking, and all of them looked at Kit.
Kit stood up, put his arm around Wren and told Dana that this was his girlfriend. Dana looked surprised, and then her smile became a little too wide.
Later, Dana found Wren alone and spoke to her kindly. She said that Kit was a good man, but he never told you what he felt, and she had waited two years.
That evening Wren asked Kit why he never talked about what he felt. He said it was none of her business, and they argued, but it did not feel like a game any more.
The next day, Leo came home with a broken bike and a very sad face. Wren and Kit forgot about their quarrel and mended it together on the garage floor, while Leo handed them tools.
That night a storm cut the power in the whole street. They cooked soup on a small stove and ate it by candlelight, and Leo soon fell asleep on the sofa.
They stood very close in the dark kitchen, and for a long moment neither of them moved. Then Wren whispered the word rules, and Kit stepped back and nodded.
In the morning, Wren went to the bookshop and told Marta everything. Marta said that she had known it from the beginning, and she asked what Wren was going to do about it.
Kit worked in his shed for three evenings and built a small desk from driftwood. He gave it to Wren and said that it was for her drawings, and that it was not part of the act.
The date of the interview came, and it was the Friday before the Lantern Fair. Wren had not told Kit about the job, and now she did not know how to start.
At last she told him about the job in Barrowfield. Kit said that he was happy for her and that she must go, but his voice sounded flat.
Aunt Dot found Wren in the garden and said, with a twinkle, that Kit looked at her like she was a lighthouse. Wren said it was only for show, and Dot only smiled and said nothing more.
In the town hall, everyone painted paper lanterns for the fair. Wren and Kit sat at the same table, and each of them painted a secret wish on the inside, where nobody could see.
On Friday morning, Wren took the early train to Barrowfield. The city was loud and fast, and she felt very small as she walked through the crowds.
Ms Halden looked at her drawings for a long time and then smiled warmly. She offered Wren the job there and then, and she asked for an answer within a week.
When the train arrived, Kit was waiting on the platform with an umbrella. She had not told him when she was coming, but he had checked every train, and she was very moved.
Kit asked how the interview had gone, and Wren said that she had to think about it. He said quietly that he would never ask her to stay, and she hoped, secretly, that he would.
A few days later they quarrelled in the café, in front of everyone. Wren said that maybe it had all been pretend anyway, and Kit answered coldly that rule one said there would be no feelings.
The next morning, Leo knocked on her door with a drawing in his hand. It showed Wren, Kit and Leo together, and he asked in a small voice if she was still coming to the fair.
Kit sat alone in the ferry shed, and old Mr Pell came in with a flask of tea. He sat down next to him and said, kindly, that he was a fool, and that everyone could see it.
Aunt Dot came to Wren's cottage with a box of old letters. She told her own love story, and she said that she had only ever wanted her niece to stop hiding from life.
That night Wren wrote an email to Ms Halden, and it was the bravest thing she had ever done. She said that she would take the job, but only if she could work from her little studio in Salt Cove.
At last it was the night of the Lantern Fair, and the whole town came to the beach. Hundreds of lanterns glowed in the dusk, and Wren walked through the crowd looking for Kit.
Kit found her at the edge of the water, holding the old napkin in his hand. He read the rules aloud, one by one, and then he said that he was crossing them all out.
Kit said that he had never been good at saying what he felt, but he was going to try. He told her that he had stopped pretending a long time ago, and that he did not want her to go.
Wren said that she had stopped pretending long ago, too, and that she was already staying. They kissed, and all around them the lanterns floated out over the dark water.
The next spring, the old napkin hung in a frame on the wall of Pell's Café. Wren worked at her driftwood desk by the sea window, and Kit hummed happily nearby while Leo drew dragons.
C1C2: Every morning Wren Ashby carried her sketchbook to the same window table in Pell's Café and filled it with foxes, owls and sleepy lighthouses for other people's children. Salt Cove was a tiny town clinging to a curve of the sea, and she loved its gulls, its salt wind and its stubborn little harbour. What she did not love was how many of its people felt entitled to arrange her life.

Wren's Aunt Dot swept into the café in a scarf the colour of marmalade, brandishing a sheet of paper as if it were a royal decree. On it, in her large and cheerful writing, were the names of five perfectly nice young men, any one of whom she considered ideal for her niece. Dot had been matchmaking for thirty years, and she was not a woman who gave up.

Dot announced, with the satisfaction of a general who has already won, that she had arranged for Wren to have dinner that very evening with the new vet. No one had asked Wren, naturally, and she felt the heat climb from her collar to her hairline. It was the fourth such dinner this year, and each had ended with her fleeing early.

At that very moment the café door swung open, and Kit Navarro walked in with oil on his hands and a smear of grease across one cheek. He was the quiet mechanic who kept the little ferry Gannet running, a man of few words who had come in only for a cup of strong coffee. He had no idea that his quiet life was about to be turned completely upside down by one frightened sentence.

In a moment of pure panic, Wren heard her own voice declare that she was already seeing someone and that there was no need for any vets. When Dot asked, with eyebrows raised, who this mystery man might be, Wren could think of only one answer, and she pointed straight at the man by the counter. Kit, holding his coffee, looked as though a large wave had just hit him from behind, and for a moment he forgot how to blink.

Kit stood perfectly still for what felt like an hour, and Wren was certain that he would deny everything and leave. Instead he crossed the café, rested a warm hand on her shoulder and said, in a voice as smooth as a calm sea, hello, darling. Dot clapped her hands together and looked so delighted that Wren felt a stab of guilt.

Dot, glowing with triumph, invited them both to Sunday lunch at once and added that the entire town would, of course, meet Kit at the Lantern Fair. That happy night was exactly six weeks away, she said, which was just enough time for everyone to get used to the wonderful news. Wren smiled and nodded and thanked her aunt, and she went on smiling until her face began to hurt.

Out on the pavement Wren apologised so many times that she lost count, explaining that her aunt had cornered her and that panic had made her point. Kit folded his arms and tried to look cross, but the corners of his mouth kept twitching upward, and at last he gave a short, helpless laugh. It was the first time she had ever heard him laugh, and it was a better sound than she had expected.

After a long pause, Kit said that he would play along, on one condition: that it should help him as well. Since his fiancée had left two years earlier, the whole town had looked at him with soft, sorrowful eyes, and a pretend girlfriend might at least put an end to the pity. Wren, who knew exactly how tiresome that kind of attention could be, nodded at once and held out her hand.

They sat down at a corner table and, with great seriousness, drew up a list of rules on a paper napkin. Rule one said that no real feelings were allowed, and rule two said that they would never, under any circumstances, lie to Kit's young nephew, Leo. Wren underlined the first rule twice, and Kit watched her do it with a faint frown.

The remaining rules were practical and rather solemn: any kissing would happen only in public, and only when absolutely necessary, and the whole arrangement would end on the day after the Lantern Fair. They signed the napkin at the bottom like two diplomats agreeing to a treaty. Neither of them noticed that the ink had run slightly where Kit's thumb had touched it.

On Sunday they sat at Dot's crowded table, surrounded by roast potatoes and curious relatives, and Dot asked in her sweetest voice how the happy couple had first met. Wren and Kit looked at each other across the gravy, suddenly aware that the one thing they had forgotten to rehearse was their own beginning. The silence stretched on and on, until even the old clock on the wall seemed to lean in and listen.

Kit began to invent a story about the day Wren had dropped her sketchbook off the jetty and he had rescued it with a fishing net, and he told it with such comic timing that the whole table roared. Wren, trying to help, added details that flatly contradicted his, a blue sketchbook instead of a red one, and a morning instead of an evening. Dot's eyes narrowed behind her glasses, but she said nothing at all and simply passed the carrots.

After lunch Kit's eight-year-old nephew, Leo, tugged at Wren's sleeve and asked her directly whether she was his uncle's girlfriend. Remembering rule two, the rule about never lying to Leo, Wren crouched down and said carefully that she and Kit were good friends who were doing something secret together. Leo considered this with the gravity of a judge and then asked her to draw him a dragon.

That night an email arrived from a Ms Halden, an editor at the large publishing house of Halden and Moss in the faraway city of Barrowfield. She had seen Wren's work, she wrote, and she admired it enormously, and she wondered whether Wren might come in for an interview about a full-time position. Wren read it three times and then closed the laptop very quietly, as though it might bite.

It rained for three days, and Kit spent most of them lying under the engine of the Gannet, swearing mildly at a stubborn bolt. Wren walked down the jetty with a flask of hot tea, aware that at least half the town was watching from behind curtains, and handed it to him with a flourish. Kit took it with a look of such surprised gratitude that she nearly forgot to perform.

On Saturday they strolled through the market holding hands, since the townspeople clearly expected it, and the result was spectacularly unconvincing. Their fingers were stiff, their steps did not match, and they moved down the row of stalls like two robots who had only just learned to walk. A woman selling cheese watched them pass and covered her mouth to hide a smile.

Mr Pell of the café was shopping for lemons nearby, and he called out, loudly enough for the whole market to hear, that they were a lovely couple. Kit, remembering the rules, bent and kissed Wren briefly on the cheek, and the stallholders burst into applause. Afterwards both of them walked on in silence, each pretending that nothing at all had been felt.

Wren perched on an upturned bucket in the ferry shed and watched Kit tune the engine, and she noticed that he hummed under his breath whenever he was happiest. It was a faint, tuneless, contented sound, and without thinking she opened her sketchbook and began to capture the line of his shoulders, the curve of his hands. She had not drawn a person she cared about in a very long time.

When Kit discovered the sketch on the workbench, he picked it up and looked at it for such a long time that Wren began to worry. Then he said, in a voice that was rougher than usual, that nobody had ever drawn him before, and he asked whether he might keep it. She tore out the page and handed it over, and the room felt suddenly very small.

At the bookshop, Wren's oldest friend Marta looked up from the till, studied her face and remarked that she was blushing. Wren replied that it was merely warm in the shop, but Marta had known her for twenty years and had never once been fooled. She folded her arms and said that she would wait, since she had all the time in the world.

On a still, golden evening, Kit let Wren take the wheel of the Gannet and steer her slowly across the bay. He stood just behind her, explaining in his quiet voice how to turn gently against the current, and she could feel the warmth of him through the thin cloth of her shirt. She was happy, she realised, and that, she knew very well, was precisely the problem.

They sat on the harbour wall with their legs dangling over the water and talked about childhood, dreams, bad haircuts and the names of every boat in the bay. It was nearly midnight when they finally noticed the time, and both of them were astonished that two people supposedly pretending could find so much to say. Neither of them was in any hurry to go home, and neither of them said so out loud.

On Friday Dana, the woman who had once been engaged to Kit, stepped off the afternoon bus and returned to Salt Cove for a single weekend. Within an hour every person in town knew about it, and when she walked into Pell's Café the whole room fell silent and turned to look at Kit. He did what he always did under pressure, which was to fall quiet and go perfectly, impenetrably still.

Kit rose from his chair, slid an arm around Wren's waist and told Dana in a clear, level voice that this was his girlfriend. Dana's eyebrows rose, and then her smile grew a little too wide, the way a smile does when it hides some other feeling entirely. Wren leaned into him as the rules required, and discovered that it required no effort whatever.

Later, Dana caught Wren alone by the window and spoke to her, not unkindly, in a low voice. Kit was the best man she had ever known, she said, but he never told you what he truly felt, and she had waited two years to hear it. The words settled in Wren's chest like a stone, because she suspected they were true.

That evening Wren asked him, bluntly, why he never talked about what he felt, and Kit replied that it was none of her business and that the arrangement did not cover it. They argued for ten uncomfortable minutes in his kitchen, their voices rising and falling, and she realised that it did not feel like pretending any longer. It felt, absurdly, like a real quarrel between two people who cared a great deal about each other, and that frightened them both.

The next afternoon Leo wheeled his broken bicycle into the garage with a face as long as a wet weekend. Wren and Kit forgot their quarrel entirely and knelt side by side on the concrete, straightening the wheel while Leo solemnly handed them tools. When the bicycle finally rolled again, the three of them cheered, and for a moment they looked exactly like a family.

That night a gale knocked out the power for the whole street, and they cooked soup on a small camping stove in Kit's kitchen and ate it by the light of a dozen candles. Leo, worn out by the excitement, fell asleep on the sofa with a blanket up to his chin. The house grew quiet, and the storm outside seemed to wrap them in a small private world.

In the dim kitchen they found themselves standing so close that she could see the candle flames dancing in his eyes, and for a long moment neither of them moved. Then Wren, hardly breathing, whispered the single word rules, and Kit stepped back with a slow nod, as if he had been caught crossing a border. The candles flickered in the draught, and the whole house seemed to let out a long and unsteady breath.

In the morning Wren walked straight into the bookshop and confessed everything to Marta, from the napkin to the candles. Marta listened without interrupting, poured her a cup of tea and then observed, with great gentleness, that she had seen it coming from the very first week. The only question left, she said, was what Wren intended to do about it.

For three evenings Kit shut himself in his shed and, without telling anyone, built a small, beautiful desk from silver driftwood he had collected on the beach. He carried it to Wren's cottage himself and said, a little gruffly, that it was for her drawings and that it was not part of any act. She ran her fingers along the smooth grain of the wood, and for once in her life she could not think of a single thing to say.

The date for the interview arrived by email, and it was set for the Friday before the Lantern Fair, the very week the pretending was due to end. Wren had not told Kit about the job in Barrowfield, partly because she feared his indifference and partly because she feared his understanding. Now the secret sat between them like a third person at the table, and every day it grew a little heavier.

At last she told him, in a rush, about the interview and the position in the city. Kit said that he was happy for her, that it was a wonderful chance and that she must go, and he said it all in a flat, careful voice without once looking her in the eye. It was the sort of kindness that hurts, because it asks for nothing and gives nothing away.

Aunt Dot found Wren pulling weeds in the garden and remarked, with a knowing twinkle, that Kit looked at her as a sailor looks at a lighthouse in a storm. Wren replied firmly that it was all for show, and Dot merely smiled, patted her hand and went inside to put the kettle on. There are times when saying nothing is the loudest thing an aunt can do.

In the town hall the whole community gathered to paint paper lanterns for the fair, and Wren and Kit were given a table at the very back. Each of them painted a wish on the inside of a lantern, turning the paper away from the other, so that no one could see what was written there. The brushes scratched softly over the paper, and the whole room smelled of paint, tea and a strange, shared kind of hope.

On Friday morning Wren took the early train to Barrowfield, her portfolio on her knees and her stomach in knots. The city, when she reached it, was loud and grey and very fast, a place where nobody stopped to talk and the pavements seemed to pull her along. She walked through the crowds feeling small, and rather homesick, and rather brave, like a fish that has swum into the wrong ocean.

Ms Halden turned the pages of the portfolio slowly, one by one, and then looked up with a broad, warm smile and offered Wren the job on the spot. It was a wonderful position, with a good salary, a real studio and the chance to see her books in every shop in the country. All Ms Halden asked in return was an answer within a week, and she said it so kindly that Wren could hardly refuse the time.

When the train drew in at Salt Cove, Kit was standing on the wet platform with an umbrella in his hand and rain on his shoulders. She had never told him which train she would take, and she understood slowly that he had met every one since noon. Her heart turned over in her chest, and she stood there in the rain with her bag in her hand, unable to find a single word.

Walking home under the umbrella, Kit asked how the interview had gone, and Wren said that she was still thinking it over. He told her quietly that whatever she chose, he would never ask her to stay, because he had once held on to someone who wanted to go and he had learned not to do it again. She had secretly hoped for exactly the opposite, and she was ashamed of how much she wanted to be asked.

Three days later the strain broke in the middle of Pell's Café, in front of a dozen customers and a very interested Mr Pell. Wren said, more sharply than she meant, that perhaps it had all been pretend anyway, and Kit answered in a voice as cold as seawater that rule one had always been no feelings. Then he walked out, leaving the door swinging and the whole room staring at her.

The next morning there was a small knock at her door, and Leo stood on the step holding a crumpled drawing in both hands. It showed three stick figures under a sky full of lanterns, Wren, Kit and himself, all holding hands, and he asked in a very small voice whether she was still coming to the fair. She knelt, hugged him hard and promised nothing, because she did not trust her own voice.

Kit sat alone in the ferry shed that evening, and old Mr Pell came in carrying a flask of tea and wearing an unusually serious face. He sat down on an upturned crate and told him, with great kindness, that he was a stubborn fool, and that everyone in Salt Cove had seen how he looked at Wren from the first day. Kit stared at the floor for a long time, and then he did something he rarely did: he did not argue, and he did not hide.

Aunt Dot arrived at the cottage with a shoebox of faded letters tied up in ribbon, and she told Wren, at last, the story of her own long, tangled love, which had begun with a mistake and a stubborn pride. She admitted that she had known from the first day that the romance was a pretence, and that she had never meant to push Wren into marriage, only out of hiding. A brave heart, she said, is still the best thing a person can own.

That night Wren sat at the driftwood desk and wrote an email to Ms Halden, choosing every word with care. She said that she would be delighted to accept the position, but only if she could work from her little studio in Salt Cove and travel to Barrowfield once a month. It was the first time she had ever asked for exactly what she wanted, and her hands shook as she pressed the button.

At last the night of the Lantern Fair arrived, and the whole of Salt Cove poured down to the beach as the sun went down in streaks of rose and gold. Hundreds of paper lanterns glowed in the dusk, bobbing in people's hands like small captured stars, and Wren moved through the crowd searching every face for one in particular. Her heart beat so loudly that she was sure the whole bay could hear it.

Kit found her at the edge of the water at last, holding the old napkin, now soft and creased from being carried in his pocket for six weeks. He read the rules aloud one by one in his steady voice, and then, with a pencil, he crossed each of them out as the crowd began to turn and listen. When he reached rule one, the last and the most important, the pencil was shaking so badly in his hand that he had to steady it with the other.

Kit said, in a voice that carried across the silent beach, that he had never been any good at saying what he felt, but that he intended to learn that night. He told her that he had stopped pretending weeks ago, that every public kiss had been a private truth, and that although he would never ask her to stay, he wished with all his heart that she would. The whole beach, with its hundreds of glowing lanterns and its hundreds of listening faces, held its breath.

Wren said that she had stopped pretending long ago as well, and that she was not going anywhere, because her new job could be done from the best studio in the world. They kissed then, at the edge of the sea, while the town cheered and the lanterns drifted out across the dark bay like a thousand small wishes finally set free. Somewhere behind them, Aunt Dot was crying happily into her marmalade-coloured scarf, and Mr Pell was cheering as loudly as he possibly could.

By the following spring, the old napkin hung in a neat frame on the wall of Pell's Café, where Mr Pell showed it proudly to every visitor and told the story at great length. Wren worked contentedly at her driftwood desk in the studio above the harbour, while Kit hummed over an engine below and Leo drew dragons on the floor between them. Aunt Dot, passing the window, only smiled and said that she had told them so.
